text.p: (Compiled for Reuters by Media Monitors)
THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

As the Federal Government makes funding cuts to higher education, universities are being forced to find new sources of income, creating tough new competition for other Australian businesses. Some universities now earn about half their income from the private sector and by 2000, the average level of dependence on Federal funding is expected to be well below 50 per cent. Page 1.

Environment Minister Robert Hill confirmed yesterday the Federal Government would allow mining and exploration in forest reserves under a two-tier system. Mining would be allowed in those reserves classed as "informal", that are deemed to have conservation values that are not as great, whereas development would still be banned in the higher tier of "dedicated" reserves. Page 2.

The Federal Government's A$250 million regional telecommunications infrastructure fund, announced last week, will come under scrutiny by National and Liberal party backbenchers from rural areas this week. In a deal with independent senators Brian Harradie and Mal Colston, the fund was set up to allocate money according to the percentage of each State's population found outside the capital city. Page 3.

The Construction, Forestry, Mining and Energy Union appears set to go ahead with a national coal strike on Wednesday, based on the understanding that the New South Wales Treasury has vetoed a proposal to finance a multi-million dollar loan to allow work to resume at Denehurst Pty Ltd's loss-making Metropolitan colliery on the State's South Coast. Page 5.
THE AUSTRALIAN

Deputy Prime Minister and Trade Minister Tim Fischer will today address the inaugural World Trade Organisation ministerial meeting in Singapore, and is likely to call on the world's leading trade countries to agree to a new "millennium" round of multilateal free-trade talks in 1999. Fischer will claim global free trade is a defence against a growing challenge from regional approaches to trade liberalisation. Page 1.

Federal Treasurer Peter Costello is planning to use the Keating Government's L.A.W. tax cuts to fund family savings incentives in the May 1997 Budget. A report by a special interdepartmental committee to Costello looked into options for promoting savings and studied similar plans in Canada, Britain and the United States. The report will be the basis of a Cabinet submission in early 1997. Page 1.

Senior Federal Government sources said they believed there are hopes up to A$10 billion will be raised from the sale of one-third of Telstra, A$2 billion more than was budgeted during the last Federal election. A windfall on Telstra would increase the Goernment's spending options in the run-up to the next election. Page 3.

Federal Environment Minister Robert Hill said on Channel 9's Sunday program that mining in the Kakadu National Park will not be introduced, despite reports to the contrary, because the Park was protected by law. Hill added that the Federal Government
wascommitted to a national reserve system of forests, with a dedicated reserve area. Page 3.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

Tasmanian Independent Senator Brian Harradine has crushed the hopes of the Australian Democrats and the Federal Opposition by saying he will not change his vote on the partial privatisation of telecommunications giant Telstra in Parliament today. However Harradine has stated he will not support any more than one-third of Telstra being sold. Page 1.

Research by Associate Professor Catherine Smith of the Department of Management at Edith Cowan University in Western Australia and the University's Deputy Vice-Chancellor Professor Leonie Still has found Australia's biggest companies are filling up overseas posts with men who are less competent than existing female executives. The study found 12 per cent of companies would rather appoint a male to work on an overseas post. Page 1. --

National Parks and Wildlife Service (NPWS) rangers are using 330 megalitres of water from a precious water bank each day to try to foster the Macquarie Marshes' biggest breeding of waterbirds since the floods of 1990. The breeding attempts come amidst deate over the New South Wales Government's management of the area between the NPWS and the cotton industry. Page 1.

New Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Commission chairman Gatjil Djerrkura has foreshadowed radical change for the body, which includes talks with Federal Independent MP Pauline Hanson, a new emphasis on the needs of traditional
Aborigines, and tighter links with the Federal Government. Page 1.
THE AGE

At least 25,000 people marched through central Melbourne yesterday in one of Australia's largest anti-racism rallies. The march, organised by People for Racial Equality, was addressed by former Victorian Liberal Premier Sir Rupert Hamer and former Victoran Labor Premier John Cain. Page A1.

Former footballer and commentator Tommy Lahiff, 86, died yesterday evening after undergoing emergency heart surgery at Box Hill Hospital. Lahiff played for Essendon, South Melbourne and Hawthorn in the then VFL and in the late 1950s joined Harry Beitzel alling matches on radio 3KZ. Page A1.

Luke Hamilton, 19, was stabbed through the heart with a knife and killed when he dropped in on a party inside the St James Anglican Church community hall in Thornbury on Saturday to check that his sister had arrived safely at the party. Only one person has come forward to say he saw the attack, although
Detective Sergeant Gavan Ryan from the homicide squad believes at least 20 people were outside when the attack occurred. Page A1.

Senior Liberal MP and Victorian Legislative Council president Bruce Chamberlain yesterday placed himself at odds with Victorian Premier Jeff Kennett by voicing his support for the A$80 million renovations to Parliament House, saying he hoped they would prceed. Page A1.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 373-1800
